title: The Apple Never Hit Newton's Head #shorts
description:
An apple fell on Isaac Newton's head and — bonk — gravity. Except it never hit him.

The apple is probably real: Newton told his friend William Stukeley he was sitting in the garden at his family farm, where he'd gone to escape the plague, when an apple fell and made him wonder why things always fall straight down — and whether the same pull reaches the Moon. Nothing in his version hits his head; storytellers and cartoons added the bonk later. Gravity didn't come in a flash either: he worked on it for about 20 years before the Principia came out in 1687. The tree is still growing at Woolsthorpe Manor.

Animated, voiced and scored in code. Narration is a synthetic (text-to-speech) voice.

title: Caesar Probably Never Said "Et Tu, Brute?" #shorts
description:
On the Ides of March, 44 BC, Julius Caesar sees Brutus among his killers and gasps "Et tu, Brute?" Probably not — that line comes from Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, written in 1599.

Suetonius says Caesar said nothing at all, just groaned, though he notes some people claimed Caesar said in Greek "kai su, teknon?" — "You too, child?" Plutarch says that when Caesar saw Brutus he simply pulled his toga over his head. He was stabbed 23 times, and a doctor said only one wound was fatal. The Latin line appears in English plays before Shakespeare; he just made it famous. Caesar's real last words? Nobody knows.

title: Ben Franklin Never Proposed the Turkey #shorts
description:
Ben Franklin wanted the turkey as America's national bird. He didn't.

In 1776 Franklin was on the committee designing the Great Seal, and his idea was Moses parting the Red Sea — no turkey. The bald eagle went on the seal in 1782. The turkey story comes from a 1784 letter to his daughter Sarah, where he joked that the Society of the Cincinnati's eagle badge looked more like a turkey, called the bald eagle "a bird of bad moral character" that steals fish from other birds, and praised the turkey as "much more respectable" — a bird of courage that would attack a British Grenadier in a red coat. It was a private, mostly joking letter. He never asked Congress for a turkey.

title: Knights Didn't Need Cranes to Get on Horses #shorts
description:
Medieval knights wore armor so heavy they had to be winched onto their horses — and if they fell, they were stuck like a turtle. Nope.

A full suit of battle armor weighed roughly 15–25 kg, less than many modern soldiers carry, and the weight was spread over the whole body. Knights trained in it from a young age and could run, roll, get back up and mount a horse unaided; the French knight Boucicaut was said to vault into the saddle in full armor. The crane image comes largely from Laurence Olivier's 1944 film Henry V, which showed knights being lowered onto their horses. Heavier jousting armor existed, but that was for sport — and still no cranes.
